narrative:
The model predicted a 76% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also worked against you; a third-decile placement falls well below the sixth-decile average of successful applicants.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 38, you scored slightly above the average of accepted students, which gave the model some reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the clear academic-ranking concerns.

You should consider reapplying after improving your academic record, perhaps by taking additional coursework that raises your class standing or by gaining targeted bar-prep experience that demonstrates stronger readiness. Strengthening those performance indicators will directly address the factors that most affected this outcome. (218 words)
